case_info.scenario: A 60-year-old man incarcerated in Ohio presented to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. He reported recent exposure to COVID-19 but had no fevers, chest pain, cough, dyspnea, or diarrhea. He had unintentionally lost 13.6 kg over 2 years. His temperature was 37 °C (98.5 °F); blood pressure, 124/75 mm Hg; pulse, 123/min; respiratory rate, 22/min; and oxygen saturation, 96% on room air. Findings on physical examination were unremarkable. His white blood cell count was 3300/μL (reference, 4500-11 000/μL) with an absolute lymphocyte count of 200/μL (reference, 1000-4800/μL). Chest radiograph showed bilateral reticulonodular opacities. He was hospitalized and treated with azithromycin, remdesivir, and dexamethasone despite 3 negative SARS-CoV-2 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test results. Two days after hospital discharge, he presented to the emergency department with recurrent syncope. His temperature was 38.1 °C (100.6 °F); blood pressure, 122/82 mm Hg; pulse, 135/min; and oxygen saturation, 86% on room air. A computed tomography scan revealed diffuse bilateral pulmonary micronodular opacities, a 2.2-cm nodule in the lingula, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy (Figure 1). Results of HIV testing were positive for HIV-1 antibodies.

case_info.explanation: A. Check urine and serumHistoplasmaantigen test results The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypoxemia and diffuse micronodular pulmonary opacities in a patient with HIV is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis. A positron emission tomography scan (choice B) is not recommended because it will not provide a definitive diagnosis. Less invasive testing should be pursued prior to bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy (choice C). The imaging findings were inconsistent with bacterial pneumonia, so intravenous antibiotics (choice D) are not indicated. Histoplasma capsulatumis a soil-based fungus associated with bird and bat droppings.1Exposure occurs via inhalation of fungal spores.1While endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, all US continental states have documented cases of histoplasmosis.2﻿H capsulatumis endemic in Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and South/Southeast Asia.3Most patients with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited cough and remain undiagnosed.4However, severe pneumonia can occur, especially in patients with immunosuppression or who inhale a large quantity of spores.4Infants and adults older than 55 years are at higher risk of severe histoplasmosis. Risk factors for dissemination include HIV with CD4 cell count less than 150/mm3, immunosuppressive medications (eg, corticosteroids, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), hematologic malignancies, and solid organ transplantation.4Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis typically have fever, fatigue, weight loss, and shortness of breath, and may also have diarrhea, headaches, altered mental status, and rash.5,6Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver enzyme and lactodehydrogenase levels.5The differential diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis includes tuberculosis, cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, malignancy, and sarcoidosis.5,6 To diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis, serum and urine tests forHistoplasmaantigen are the tests of choice and have sensitivities of 95% and specificities of 97%.7Disseminated histoplasmosis is fatal if untreated.5Mild to moderate disseminated histoplasmosis is treated with 200 mg of oral itraconazole 3 times daily, followed by twice-daily dosing for 12 months.7,8For severe disseminated histoplasmosis (eg, respiratory, circulatory, or kidney failure; neurologic signs; coagulation abnormalities; or symptoms that limit self-care), induction therapy consists of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, or for 4 to 6 weeks if there is central nervous system (CNS) involvement.7,8Recommended maintenance therapy is oral itraconazole for 12 months to lifelong, depending on risk of reinfection or relapse, which occurs most commonly in patients with CNS disease.7,8Mortality rates in patients with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis range from 10% to 60%, depending on access to care.9 The patient’s urineHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 25 ng/mL and serumHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 20.0 ng/mL (reference positive, >0.20 ng/mL for both). Serum testing revealed negative T-spot, negativeCryptococcusantigen, and negativeCoccidioidesantibody findings. Results ofMycobacterium tuberculosisPCR andPneumocystis jiroveciipneumonia PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid were negative. Results of brain magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid cell count, differential, total protein level, and glucose level were normal. HIV viral load was 3.9 million copies/mL, and CD4 cell count was 15/mm3. The patient was treated with 3 days of oral itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), followed by twice-daily dosing. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 10. On discharge, results of fungal, blood, BAL, and acid-fast bacillus cultures and cerebrospinal fluidHistoplasmaantigen testing were pending. He was to continue ART, itraconazole (200 mg twice daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg 3 times per week) forP jiroveciipneumonia prophylaxis. Twenty days later, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with headaches. Results of prior fungal blood and BAL cultures and CNSHistoplasmaantigen testing were positive but had not been reported. He received treatment for CNS histoplasmosis with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/d) for 6 weeks. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, performed to evaluate the pulmonary nodule, showed necrotizing granulomas with yeast (Figure 2). After a 44-day hospitalization, the patient was discharged taking ART, itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. In clinic 18 months later, he was asymptomatic, with a CD4 count of 182/mm3and HIV viral load of 100 copies/mL. All of his prior medications were continued, including itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) due to the high risk of reinfection or relapse associated with disseminated histoplasmosis involving the CNS, especially with CD4 cell count less than 200 cells/mm3.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload

[Important rules]

* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE

   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis

   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: A. Check urine and serumHistoplasmaantigen test results The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypoxemia and diffuse micronodular pulmonary opacities in a patient with HIV is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis. A positron emission tomography scan (choice B) is not recommended because it will not provide a definitive diagnosis. Less invasive testing should be pursued prior to bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy (choice C). The imaging findings were inconsistent with bacterial pneumonia, so intravenous antibiotics (choice D) are not indicated. Histoplasma capsulatumis a soil-based fungus associated with bird and bat droppings.1Exposure occurs via inhalation of fungal spores.1While endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, all US continental states have documented cases of histoplasmosis.2﻿H capsulatumis endemic in Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and South/Southeast Asia.3Most patients with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited cough and remain undiagnosed.4However, severe pneumonia can occur, especially in patients with immunosuppression or who inhale a large quantity of spores.4Infants and adults older than 55 years are at higher risk of severe histoplasmosis. Risk factors for dissemination include HIV with CD4 cell count less than 150/mm3, immunosuppressive medications (eg, corticosteroids, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), hematologic malignancies, and solid organ transplantation.4Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis typically have fever, fatigue, weight loss, and shortness of breath, and may also have diarrhea, headaches, altered mental status, and rash.5,6Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver enzyme and lactodehydrogenase levels.5The differential diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis includes tuberculosis, cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, malignancy, and sarcoidosis.5,6 To diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis, serum and urine tests forHistoplasmaantigen are the tests of choice and have sensitivities of 95% and specificities of 97%.7Disseminated histoplasmosis is fatal if untreated.5Mild to moderate disseminated histoplasmosis is treated with 200 mg of oral itraconazole 3 times daily, followed by twice-daily dosing for 12 months.7,8For severe disseminated histoplasmosis (eg, respiratory, circulatory, or kidney failure; neurologic signs; coagulation abnormalities; or symptoms that limit self-care), induction therapy consists of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, or for 4 to 6 weeks if there is central nervous system (CNS) involvement.7,8Recommended maintenance therapy is oral itraconazole for 12 months to lifelong, depending on risk of reinfection or relapse, which occurs most commonly in patients with CNS disease.7,8Mortality rates in patients with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis range from 10% to 60%, depending on access to care.9 The patient’s urineHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 25 ng/mL and serumHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 20.0 ng/mL (reference positive, >0.20 ng/mL for both). Serum testing revealed negative T-spot, negativeCryptococcusantigen, and negativeCoccidioidesantibody findings. Results ofMycobacterium tuberculosisPCR andPneumocystis jiroveciipneumonia PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid were negative. Results of brain magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid cell count, differential, total protein level, and glucose level were normal. HIV viral load was 3.9 million copies/mL, and CD4 cell count was 15/mm3. The patient was treated with 3 days of oral itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), followed by twice-daily dosing. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 10. On discharge, results of fungal, blood, BAL, and acid-fast bacillus cultures and cerebrospinal fluidHistoplasmaantigen testing were pending. He was to continue ART, itraconazole (200 mg twice daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg 3 times per week) forP jiroveciipneumonia prophylaxis. Twenty days later, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with headaches. Results of prior fungal blood and BAL cultures and CNSHistoplasmaantigen testing were positive but had not been reported. He received treatment for CNS histoplasmosis with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/d) for 6 weeks. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, performed to evaluate the pulmonary nodule, showed necrotizing granulomas with yeast (Figure 2). After a 44-day hospitalization, the patient was discharged taking ART, itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. In clinic 18 months later, he was asymptomatic, with a CD4 count of 182/mm3and HIV viral load of 100 copies/mL. All of his prior medications were continued, including itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) due to the high risk of reinfection or relapse associated with disseminated histoplasmosis involving the CNS, especially with CD4 cell count less than 200 cells/mm3.

He was hospitalized and treated with azithromycin, remdesivir, and dexamethasone despite 3 negative SARS-CoV-2 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test results. Two days after hospital discharge, he presented to the emergency department with recurrent syncope. His temperature was 38.1 °C (100.6 °F); blood pressure, 122/82 mm Hg; pulse, 135/min; and oxygen saturation, 86% on room air. [Output Format]

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or
  relevant evidence — not mere disagreement or reframing.

  when a point has merit even if you do not fully concede.

[Cognitive Burden]

- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 2.8. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.

case_info.explanation: A. Check urine and serumHistoplasmaantigen test results The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypoxemia and diffuse micronodular pulmonary opacities in a patient with HIV is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis. A positron emission tomography scan (choice B) is not recommended because it will not provide a definitive diagnosis. Less invasive testing should be pursued prior to bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy (choice C). The imaging findings were inconsistent with bacterial pneumonia, so intravenous antibiotics (choice D) are not indicated. Histoplasma capsulatumis a soil-based fungus associated with bird and bat droppings.1Exposure occurs via inhalation of fungal spores.1While endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, all US continental states have documented cases of histoplasmosis.2﻿H capsulatumis endemic in Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and South/Southeast Asia.3Most patients with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited cough and remain undiagnosed.4However, severe pneumonia can occur, especially in patients with immunosuppression or who inhale a large quantity of spores.4Infants and adults older than 55 years are at higher risk of severe histoplasmosis. Risk factors for dissemination include HIV with CD4 cell count less than 150/mm3, immunosuppressive medications (eg, corticosteroids, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), hematologic malignancies, and solid organ transplantation.4Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis typically have fever, fatigue, weight loss, and shortness of breath, and may also have diarrhea, headaches, altered mental status, and rash.5,6Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver enzyme and lactodehydrogenase levels.5The differential diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis includes tuberculosis, cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, malignancy, and sarcoidosis.5,6 To diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis, serum and urine tests forHistoplasmaantigen are the tests of choice and have sensitivities of 95% and specificities of 97%.7Disseminated histoplasmosis is fatal if untreated.5Mild to moderate disseminated histoplasmosis is treated with 200 mg of oral itraconazole 3 times daily, followed by twice-daily dosing for 12 months.7,8For severe disseminated histoplasmosis (eg, respiratory, circulatory, or kidney failure; neurologic signs; coagulation abnormalities; or symptoms that limit self-care), induction therapy consists of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, or for 4 to 6 weeks if there is central nervous system (CNS) involvement.7,8Recommended maintenance therapy is oral itraconazole for 12 months to lifelong, depending on risk of reinfection or relapse, which occurs most commonly in patients with CNS disease.7,8Mortality rates in patients with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis range from 10% to 60%, depending on access to care.9 The patient’s urineHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 25 ng/mL and serumHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 20.0 ng/mL (reference positive, >0.20 ng/mL for both). Serum testing revealed negative T-spot, negativeCryptococcusantigen, and negativeCoccidioidesantibody findings. Results ofMycobacterium tuberculosisPCR andPneumocystis jiroveciipneumonia PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid were negative. Results of brain magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid cell count, differential, total protein level, and glucose level were normal. HIV viral load was 3.9 million copies/mL, and CD4 cell count was 15/mm3. The patient was treated with 3 days of oral itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), followed by twice-daily dosing. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 10. On discharge, results of fungal, blood, BAL, and acid-fast bacillus cultures and cerebrospinal fluidHistoplasmaantigen testing were pending. He was to continue ART, itraconazole (200 mg twice daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg 3 times per week) forP jiroveciipneumonia prophylaxis. Twenty days later, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with headaches. Results of prior fungal blood and BAL cultures and CNSHistoplasmaantigen testing were positive but had not been reported. He received treatment for CNS histoplasmosis with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/d) for 6 weeks. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, performed to evaluate the pulmonary nodule, showed necrotizing granulomas with yeast (Figure 2). After a 44-day hospitalization, the patient was discharged taking ART, itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. In clinic 18 months later, he was asymptomatic, with a CD4 count of 182/mm3and HIV viral load of 100 copies/mL. All of his prior medications were continued, including itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) due to the high risk of reinfection or relapse associated with disseminated histoplasmosis involving the CNS, especially with CD4 cell count less than 200 cells/mm3.

case_info.explanation: A. Check urine and serumHistoplasmaantigen test results The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypoxemia and diffuse micronodular pulmonary opacities in a patient with HIV is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis. A positron emission tomography scan (choice B) is not recommended because it will not provide a definitive diagnosis. Less invasive testing should be pursued prior to bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy (choice C). The imaging findings were inconsistent with bacterial pneumonia, so intravenous antibiotics (choice D) are not indicated. Histoplasma capsulatumis a soil-based fungus associated with bird and bat droppings.1Exposure occurs via inhalation of fungal spores.1While endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, all US continental states have documented cases of histoplasmosis.2﻿H capsulatumis endemic in Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and South/Southeast Asia.3Most patients with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited cough and remain undiagnosed.4However, severe pneumonia can occur, especially in patients with immunosuppression or who inhale a large quantity of spores.4Infants and adults older than 55 years are at higher risk of severe histoplasmosis. Risk factors for dissemination include HIV with CD4 cell count less than 150/mm3, immunosuppressive medications (eg, corticosteroids, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), hematologic malignancies, and solid organ transplantation.4Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis typically have fever, fatigue, weight loss, and shortness of breath, and may also have diarrhea, headaches, altered mental status, and rash.5,6Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver enzyme and lactodehydrogenase levels.5The differential diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis includes tuberculosis, cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, malignancy, and sarcoidosis.5,6 To diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis, serum and urine tests forHistoplasmaantigen are the tests of choice and have sensitivities of 95% and specificities of 97%.7Disseminated histoplasmosis is fatal if untreated.5Mild to moderate disseminated histoplasmosis is treated with 200 mg of oral itraconazole 3 times daily, followed by twice-daily dosing for 12 months.7,8For severe disseminated histoplasmosis (eg, respiratory, circulatory, or kidney failure; neurologic signs; coagulation abnormalities; or symptoms that limit self-care), induction therapy consists of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, or for 4 to 6 weeks if there is central nervous system (CNS) involvement.7,8Recommended maintenance therapy is oral itraconazole for 12 months to lifelong, depending on risk of reinfection or relapse, which occurs most commonly in patients with CNS disease.7,8Mortality rates in patients with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis range from 10% to 60%, depending on access to care.9 The patient’s urineHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 25 ng/mL and serumHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 20.0 ng/mL (reference positive, >0.20 ng/mL for both). Serum testing revealed negative T-spot, negativeCryptococcusantigen, and negativeCoccidioidesantibody findings. Results ofMycobacterium tuberculosisPCR andPneumocystis jiroveciipneumonia PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid were negative. Results of brain magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid cell count, differential, total protein level, and glucose level were normal. HIV viral load was 3.9 million copies/mL, and CD4 cell count was 15/mm3. The patient was treated with 3 days of oral itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), followed by twice-daily dosing. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 10. On discharge, results of fungal, blood, BAL, and acid-fast bacillus cultures and cerebrospinal fluidHistoplasmaantigen testing were pending. He was to continue ART, itraconazole (200 mg twice daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg 3 times per week) forP jiroveciipneumonia prophylaxis. Twenty days later, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with headaches. Results of prior fungal blood and BAL cultures and CNSHistoplasmaantigen testing were positive but had not been reported. He received treatment for CNS histoplasmosis with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/d) for 6 weeks. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, performed to evaluate the pulmonary nodule, showed necrotizing granulomas with yeast (Figure 2). After a 44-day hospitalization, the patient was discharged taking ART, itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. In clinic 18 months later, he was asymptomatic, with a CD4 count of 182/mm3and HIV viral load of 100 copies/mL. All of his prior medications were continued, including itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) due to the high risk of reinfection or relapse associated with disseminated histoplasmosis involving the CNS, especially with CD4 cell count less than 200 cells/mm3.

case_info.explanation: A. Check urine and serumHistoplasmaantigen test results The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypoxemia and diffuse micronodular pulmonary opacities in a patient with HIV is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis. A positron emission tomography scan (choice B) is not recommended because it will not provide a definitive diagnosis. Less invasive testing should be pursued prior to bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy (choice C). The imaging findings were inconsistent with bacterial pneumonia, so intravenous antibiotics (choice D) are not indicated. Histoplasma capsulatumis a soil-based fungus associated with bird and bat droppings.1Exposure occurs via inhalation of fungal spores.1While endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, all US continental states have documented cases of histoplasmosis.2﻿H capsulatumis endemic in Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and South/Southeast Asia.3Most patients with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited cough and remain undiagnosed.4However, severe pneumonia can occur, especially in patients with immunosuppression or who inhale a large quantity of spores.4Infants and adults older than 55 years are at higher risk of severe histoplasmosis. Risk factors for dissemination include HIV with CD4 cell count less than 150/mm3, immunosuppressive medications (eg, corticosteroids, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), hematologic malignancies, and solid organ transplantation.4Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis typically have fever, fatigue, weight loss, and shortness of breath, and may also have diarrhea, headaches, altered mental status, and rash.5,6Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver enzyme and lactodehydrogenase levels.5The differential diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis includes tuberculosis, cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, malignancy, and sarcoidosis.5,6 To diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis, serum and urine tests forHistoplasmaantigen are the tests of choice and have sensitivities of 95% and specificities of 97%.7Disseminated histoplasmosis is fatal if untreated.5Mild to moderate disseminated histoplasmosis is treated with 200 mg of oral itraconazole 3 times daily, followed by twice-daily dosing for 12 months.7,8For severe disseminated histoplasmosis (eg, respiratory, circulatory, or kidney failure; neurologic signs; coagulation abnormalities; or symptoms that limit self-care), induction therapy consists of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, or for 4 to 6 weeks if there is central nervous system (CNS) involvement.7,8Recommended maintenance therapy is oral itraconazole for 12 months to lifelong, depending on risk of reinfection or relapse, which occurs most commonly in patients with CNS disease.7,8Mortality rates in patients with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis range from 10% to 60%, depending on access to care.9 The patient’s urineHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 25 ng/mL and serumHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 20.0 ng/mL (reference positive, >0.20 ng/mL for both). Serum testing revealed negative T-spot, negativeCryptococcusantigen, and negativeCoccidioidesantibody findings. Results ofMycobacterium tuberculosisPCR andPneumocystis jiroveciipneumonia PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid were negative. Results of brain magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid cell count, differential, total protein level, and glucose level were normal. HIV viral load was 3.9 million copies/mL, and CD4 cell count was 15/mm3. The patient was treated with 3 days of oral itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), followed by twice-daily dosing. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 10. On discharge, results of fungal, blood, BAL, and acid-fast bacillus cultures and cerebrospinal fluidHistoplasmaantigen testing were pending. He was to continue ART, itraconazole (200 mg twice daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg 3 times per week) forP jiroveciipneumonia prophylaxis. Twenty days later, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with headaches. Results of prior fungal blood and BAL cultures and CNSHistoplasmaantigen testing were positive but had not been reported. He received treatment for CNS histoplasmosis with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/d) for 6 weeks. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, performed to evaluate the pulmonary nodule, showed necrotizing granulomas with yeast (Figure 2). After a 44-day hospitalization, the patient was discharged taking ART, itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. In clinic 18 months later, he was asymptomatic, with a CD4 count of 182/mm3and HIV viral load of 100 copies/mL. All of his prior medications were continued, including itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) due to the high risk of reinfection or relapse associated with disseminated histoplasmosis involving the CNS, especially with CD4 cell count less than 200 cells/mm3.

case_info.explanation: A. Check urine and serumHistoplasmaantigen test results The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypoxemia and diffuse micronodular pulmonary opacities in a patient with HIV is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis. A positron emission tomography scan (choice B) is not recommended because it will not provide a definitive diagnosis. Less invasive testing should be pursued prior to bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy (choice C). The imaging findings were inconsistent with bacterial pneumonia, so intravenous antibiotics (choice D) are not indicated. Histoplasma capsulatumis a soil-based fungus associated with bird and bat droppings.1Exposure occurs via inhalation of fungal spores.1While endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, all US continental states have documented cases of histoplasmosis.2﻿H capsulatumis endemic in Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and South/Southeast Asia.3Most patients with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited cough and remain undiagnosed.4However, severe pneumonia can occur, especially in patients with immunosuppression or who inhale a large quantity of spores.4Infants and adults older than 55 years are at higher risk of severe histoplasmosis. Risk factors for dissemination include HIV with CD4 cell count less than 150/mm3, immunosuppressive medications (eg, corticosteroids, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), hematologic malignancies, and solid organ transplantation.4Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis typically have fever, fatigue, weight loss, and shortness of breath, and may also have diarrhea, headaches, altered mental status, and rash.5,6Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver enzyme and lactodehydrogenase levels.5The differential diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis includes tuberculosis, cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, malignancy, and sarcoidosis.5,6 To diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis, serum and urine tests forHistoplasmaantigen are the tests of choice and have sensitivities of 95% and specificities of 97%.7Disseminated histoplasmosis is fatal if untreated.5Mild to moderate disseminated histoplasmosis is treated with 200 mg of oral itraconazole 3 times daily, followed by twice-daily dosing for 12 months.7,8For severe disseminated histoplasmosis (eg, respiratory, circulatory, or kidney failure; neurologic signs; coagulation abnormalities; or symptoms that limit self-care), induction therapy consists of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, or for 4 to 6 weeks if there is central nervous system (CNS) involvement.7,8Recommended maintenance therapy is oral itraconazole for 12 months to lifelong, depending on risk of reinfection or relapse, which occurs most commonly in patients with CNS disease.7,8Mortality rates in patients with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis range from 10% to 60%, depending on access to care.9 The patient’s urineHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 25 ng/mL and serumHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 20.0 ng/mL (reference positive, >0.20 ng/mL for both). Serum testing revealed negative T-spot, negativeCryptococcusantigen, and negativeCoccidioidesantibody findings. Results ofMycobacterium tuberculosisPCR andPneumocystis jiroveciipneumonia PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid were negative. Results of brain magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid cell count, differential, total protein level, and glucose level were normal. HIV viral load was 3.9 million copies/mL, and CD4 cell count was 15/mm3. The patient was treated with 3 days of oral itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), followed by twice-daily dosing. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 10. On discharge, results of fungal, blood, BAL, and acid-fast bacillus cultures and cerebrospinal fluidHistoplasmaantigen testing were pending. He was to continue ART, itraconazole (200 mg twice daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg 3 times per week) forP jiroveciipneumonia prophylaxis. Twenty days later, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with headaches. Results of prior fungal blood and BAL cultures and CNSHistoplasmaantigen testing were positive but had not been reported. He received treatment for CNS histoplasmosis with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/d) for 6 weeks. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, performed to evaluate the pulmonary nodule, showed necrotizing granulomas with yeast (Figure 2). After a 44-day hospitalization, the patient was discharged taking ART, itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. In clinic 18 months later, he was asymptomatic, with a CD4 count of 182/mm3and HIV viral load of 100 copies/mL. All of his prior medications were continued, including itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) due to the high risk of reinfection or relapse associated with disseminated histoplasmosis involving the CNS, especially with CD4 cell count less than 200 cells/mm3.

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before

   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.

       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.

   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:

       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.

       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."

   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.explanation: A. Check urine and serumHistoplasmaantigen test results The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypoxemia and diffuse micronodular pulmonary opacities in a patient with HIV is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis. A positron emission tomography scan (choice B) is not recommended because it will not provide a definitive diagnosis. Less invasive testing should be pursued prior to bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy (choice C). The imaging findings were inconsistent with bacterial pneumonia, so intravenous antibiotics (choice D) are not indicated. Histoplasma capsulatumis a soil-based fungus associated with bird and bat droppings.1Exposure occurs via inhalation of fungal spores.1While endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, all US continental states have documented cases of histoplasmosis.2﻿H capsulatumis endemic in Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and South/Southeast Asia.3Most patients with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited cough and remain undiagnosed.4However, severe pneumonia can occur, especially in patients with immunosuppression or who inhale a large quantity of spores.4Infants and adults older than 55 years are at higher risk of severe histoplasmosis. Risk factors for dissemination include HIV with CD4 cell count less than 150/mm3, immunosuppressive medications (eg, corticosteroids, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), hematologic malignancies, and solid organ transplantation.4Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis typically have fever, fatigue, weight loss, and shortness of breath, and may also have diarrhea, headaches, altered mental status, and rash.5,6Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver enzyme and lactodehydrogenase levels.5The differential diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis includes tuberculosis, cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, malignancy, and sarcoidosis.5,6 To diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis, serum and urine tests forHistoplasmaantigen are the tests of choice and have sensitivities of 95% and specificities of 97%.7Disseminated histoplasmosis is fatal if untreated.5Mild to moderate disseminated histoplasmosis is treated with 200 mg of oral itraconazole 3 times daily, followed by twice-daily dosing for 12 months.7,8For severe disseminated histoplasmosis (eg, respiratory, circulatory, or kidney failure; neurologic signs; coagulation abnormalities; or symptoms that limit self-care), induction therapy consists of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, or for 4 to 6 weeks if there is central nervous system (CNS) involvement.7,8Recommended maintenance therapy is oral itraconazole for 12 months to lifelong, depending on risk of reinfection or relapse, which occurs most commonly in patients with CNS disease.7,8Mortality rates in patients with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis range from 10% to 60%, depending on access to care.9 The patient’s urineHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 25 ng/mL and serumHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 20.0 ng/mL (reference positive, >0.20 ng/mL for both). Serum testing revealed negative T-spot, negativeCryptococcusantigen, and negativeCoccidioidesantibody findings. Results ofMycobacterium tuberculosisPCR andPneumocystis jiroveciipneumonia PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid were negative. Results of brain magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid cell count, differential, total protein level, and glucose level were normal. HIV viral load was 3.9 million copies/mL, and CD4 cell count was 15/mm3. The patient was treated with 3 days of oral itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), followed by twice-daily dosing. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 10. On discharge, results of fungal, blood, BAL, and acid-fast bacillus cultures and cerebrospinal fluidHistoplasmaantigen testing were pending. He was to continue ART, itraconazole (200 mg twice daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg 3 times per week) forP jiroveciipneumonia prophylaxis. Twenty days later, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with headaches. Results of prior fungal blood and BAL cultures and CNSHistoplasmaantigen testing were positive but had not been reported.        compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or

     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.

     after the AI's message.

   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."

       current conclusion may be unsafe."

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

     message.

       competing options already qualifies.

   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be

   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.

case_info.caption: Patient’s computed tomography pulmonary angiogram.
case_info.explanation: A. Check urine and serumHistoplasmaantigen test results The key to the correct diagnosis is recognizing that hypoxemia and diffuse micronodular pulmonary opacities in a patient with HIV is characteristic of disseminated histoplasmosis. A positron emission tomography scan (choice B) is not recommended because it will not provide a definitive diagnosis. Less invasive testing should be pursued prior to bronchoscopy and transbronchial biopsy (choice C). The imaging findings were inconsistent with bacterial pneumonia, so intravenous antibiotics (choice D) are not indicated. Histoplasma capsulatumis a soil-based fungus associated with bird and bat droppings.1Exposure occurs via inhalation of fungal spores.1While endemic in the Ohio and Mississippi River valleys, all US continental states have documented cases of histoplasmosis.2﻿H capsulatumis endemic in Central and South America, sub-Saharan Africa, and South/Southeast Asia.3Most patients with acute pulmonary histoplasmosis are asymptomatic or have mild, self-limited cough and remain undiagnosed.4However, severe pneumonia can occur, especially in patients with immunosuppression or who inhale a large quantity of spores.4Infants and adults older than 55 years are at higher risk of severe histoplasmosis. Risk factors for dissemination include HIV with CD4 cell count less than 150/mm3, immunosuppressive medications (eg, corticosteroids, tumor necrosis factor inhibitors), hematologic malignancies, and solid organ transplantation.4Patients with disseminated histoplasmosis typically have fever, fatigue, weight loss, and shortness of breath, and may also have diarrhea, headaches, altered mental status, and rash.5,6Common laboratory findings include anemia, thrombocytopenia, leukopenia, and elevated liver enzyme and lactodehydrogenase levels.5The differential diagnosis of disseminated histoplasmosis includes tuberculosis, cryptococcus, coccidioidomycosis, blastomycosis, malignancy, and sarcoidosis.5,6 To diagnose disseminated histoplasmosis, serum and urine tests forHistoplasmaantigen are the tests of choice and have sensitivities of 95% and specificities of 97%.7Disseminated histoplasmosis is fatal if untreated.5Mild to moderate disseminated histoplasmosis is treated with 200 mg of oral itraconazole 3 times daily, followed by twice-daily dosing for 12 months.7,8For severe disseminated histoplasmosis (eg, respiratory, circulatory, or kidney failure; neurologic signs; coagulation abnormalities; or symptoms that limit self-care), induction therapy consists of intravenous liposomal amphotericin B for 2 weeks, or for 4 to 6 weeks if there is central nervous system (CNS) involvement.7,8Recommended maintenance therapy is oral itraconazole for 12 months to lifelong, depending on risk of reinfection or relapse, which occurs most commonly in patients with CNS disease.7,8Mortality rates in patients with HIV and disseminated histoplasmosis range from 10% to 60%, depending on access to care.9 The patient’s urineHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 25 ng/mL and serumHistoplasmaantigen level was greater than 20.0 ng/mL (reference positive, >0.20 ng/mL for both). Serum testing revealed negative T-spot, negativeCryptococcusantigen, and negativeCoccidioidesantibody findings. Results ofMycobacterium tuberculosisPCR andPneumocystis jiroveciipneumonia PCR of bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid were negative. Results of brain magnetic resonance imaging were normal. Cerebrospinal fluid cell count, differential, total protein level, and glucose level were normal. HIV viral load was 3.9 million copies/mL, and CD4 cell count was 15/mm3. The patient was treated with 3 days of oral itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), followed by twice-daily dosing. Antiretroviral treatment (ART) with bictegravir-emtricitabine-tenofovir alafenamide was started on hospital day 10. On discharge, results of fungal, blood, BAL, and acid-fast bacillus cultures and cerebrospinal fluidHistoplasmaantigen testing were pending. He was to continue ART, itraconazole (200 mg twice daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (160-800 mg 3 times per week) forP jiroveciipneumonia prophylaxis. Twenty days later, the patient was readmitted to the hospital with headaches. Results of prior fungal blood and BAL cultures and CNSHistoplasmaantigen testing were positive but had not been reported. He received treatment for CNS histoplasmosis with intravenous liposomal amphotericin B (3 mg/kg/d) for 6 weeks. Bronchoscopy with transbronchial biopsy, performed to evaluate the pulmonary nodule, showed necrotizing granulomas with yeast (Figure 2). After a 44-day hospitalization, the patient was discharged taking ART, itraconazole (200 mg 3 times daily), and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole. In clinic 18 months later, he was asymptomatic, with a CD4 count of 182/mm3and HIV viral load of 100 copies/mL. All of his prior medications were continued, including itraconazole (200 mg twice daily) due to the high risk of reinfection or relapse associated with disseminated histoplasmosis involving the CNS, especially with CD4 cell count less than 200 cells/mm3.

[Case]
A 60-year-old man incarcerated in Ohio presented to the emergency department after a syncopal episode. Findings on physical examination were unremarkable. His white blood cell count was 3300/μL (reference, 4500-11 000/μL) with an absolute lymphocyte count of 200/μL (reference, 1000-4800/μL). Chest radiograph showed bilateral reticulonodular opacities. He was hospitalized and treated with azithromycin, remdesivir, and dexamethasone despite 3 negative SARS-CoV-2 polymerase chain reaction (PCR) test results. Two days after hospital discharge, he presented to the emergency department with recurrent syncope. His temperature was 38.1 °C (100.6 °F); blood pressure, 122/82 mm Hg; pulse, 135/min; and oxygen saturation, 86% on room air. A computed tomography scan revealed diffuse bilateral pulmonary micronodular opacities, a 2.2-cm nodule in the lingula, and mediastinal and hilar lymphadenopathy (Figure 1). Results of HIV testing were positive for HIV-1 antibodies.
